extraction_text: Yudhishthira expresses remorse for the sins committed during the war, driven by greed for wealth, and asks Bhishma how to eliminate greed.
Bhishma recounts an ancient story where King Janaka of Videha responds to the Brahmin Mandavya's request by singing about the nature of greed.

attributes.relationships: Bhishma narrates; King Janaka teaches Mandavya
key_points: True happiness comes from eliminating greed
One should use wealth for dharma (righteousness)

extraction_text: Mandavya, upon hearing King Janaka's words, is filled with joy, praises them, and embarks on the path to liberation (moksha).
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma what qualities, behavior, knowledge, and aspirations enable one to reach the eternal, unchanging Brahman beyond primordial matter.

attributes.relationships: Continued dialogue between Yudhishthira and Bhishma

extraction_text: Bhishma describes the practices for attaining the supreme state: love for liberation, controlled diet and senses, wandering asceticism, equanimity, non-violence, compassion, endurance, and disciplined begging.
The text describes the ideal characteristics and lifestyle of a renunciate (sannyasin).

details: Does not seek ordinary gains or guest honors
Indifferent to food quality
Lives in secluded places like empty houses, tree roots, forests, caves
Remains equanimous in pleasure and pain
Practices austerities and controls impulses of speech, mind, anger, knowledge, hunger, and lust
Remains neutral to praise and blame
Soul is noble, maintains vows, is self-controlled, unattached, calm, and meditative
Does not confuse forest life with household life
Eats unexpected food
Joy does not enter his heart

extraction_text: Hari (identified as Krishna/Vishnu) declares this lifestyle as the path to liberation for the wise.

details: This lifestyle is liberation for the wise but suffering for the foolish
By becoming a renunciate and granting fearlessness to all beings, one reaches the radiant, infinite world

extraction_text: Yudhishthira expresses his profound suffering and questions when he and his brothers will adopt the renunciate lifestyle.

details: Yudhishthira says everyone considers them (the Pandavas) fortunate, but no one suffers more
They are born human and suffer, yet are imagined as gods by the world

He asks when they will adopt the painful renunciate lifestyle, free themselves from the seventeen constituents, five elements, five sense objects, and three gunas, and abandon the kingdom like vow-keeping sages who do not undergo rebirth

extraction_text: Bhishma explains the nature of the soul, karma, and liberation through knowledge.

details: Everything in the world is limited, not infinite; even rebirth has a limit
The soul is always the master of good and evil but is surrounded by rising tamas (darkness)
Like wind carrying black dust meeting red dust appears colored, the soul—though colorless—becomes colored by karma under tamas and moves from body to body
When darkness born of ignorance is dispelled by knowledge, the eternal Brahman is revealed
Sages say Brahman is not attained by action; those who attain liberation should be worshipped by you, people, and gods; therefore, great sages constantly seek identity with Brahman

extraction_text: Bhishma prepares to tell an ancient story about the conduct of Diti's son (a Daitya/Asura) after losing his kingdom.

details: Bhishma asks Yudhishthira to listen attentively to an ancient chant—a legend about the conduct of Diti's son (a Daitya named Vritra or similar) after losing sovereignty

extraction_text: Vritra was defeated, became isolated, and lost his sovereignty.
Ushanas (Shukra) questioned the defeated Vritra about his lack of sorrow.
Vritra explained his philosophical understanding, stating he does not grieve or rejoice because he knows all beings come and go, subject to time and karma.
Vritra recounted his past: he performed great austerities, grew powerful by consuming the essence of beings, conquered the three worlds, and was radiant and invincible.
Vritra stated that during his battle with Indra, he saw the glorious deity Hari, also known as Narayana, Vishnu, etc.

Vritra, stating his remaining merit from austerities, asked Ushanas about the fruits of action: how prosperity is gained and lost, what sustains beings, what actions lead to the supreme eternal state, and through what knowledge or action that state is attained.
Bhishma narrated that the sage (Ushanas) began to answer Vritra's questions, instructing the listener (Yudhishthira) and his brothers to listen attentively.
Ushanas began his response by paying homage to Lord Vishnu, whose arms encircle the glorious earth, and announced he would describe Vishnu's supreme greatness.
The great sage Yungtong (永童), whose soul is Dharma, arrived to resolve doubts and difficulties during their conversation.
Yungtong was worshipped by the Asura King Vritra (弗栗多) and the sage Ushana (优沙那), then sat on a fine cushion.

attributes.relationships: Ushana requests Yungtong to speak to Vritra

extraction_text: Ushana asked Yungtong to narrate the supreme greatness of Vishnu (毗湿奴) to the Danava King (Vritra).
Yungtong began narrating the supreme greatness of Vishnu to the intelligent Danava King with meaningful words.

attributes.content: Description of Vishnu's nature and role

extraction_text: Yungtong explained that Vishnu creates all beings (moving and non-moving), withdraws them at the appropriate time, and releases them again; all worlds enter him during destruction and emerge from him afterward.

attributes.divine_element: Vishnu as creator, sustainer, and destroyer

extraction_text: Yungtong stated that one cannot reach Vishnu through charity, austerities, or sacrifices, but only through control of the senses.

attributes.method: Sense control as path to Vishnu

extraction_text: Yungtong described how purification is achieved through gradual accumulation of actions over hundreds of rebirths, or through great effort in a single lifetime, using analogies of goldsmith purifying gold and removing odors from seeds.
Yungtong explained that Hari (Vishnu), also known as Narayana, is beginningless and endless, creates all beings, and is the destroyer and indestructible among all beings with eleven transformations.

attributes.divine_element: Vishnu as Narayana with cosmic form

extraction_text: Yungtong described Vishnu's cosmic form: his feet are the earth, head is the sky, arms are the directions, ears are space, radiance is the sun, mind is in the moon, wisdom in knowledge, taste in water, planets in his eyebrows, stars in his eyes.

Yungtong explained that the three qualities (sattva, rajas, tamas) are attributes of Narayana, who is the exit from all stages of life and the result of all actions and inactions, the supreme unchanging one.

attributes.concepts: Three gunas, Vishnu as ultimate reality

extraction_text: Yungtong described Vishnu's manifestations: his body hair are meters, letters, and language; Dharma relies on his heart; he is Brahman, Dharma, austerities, existence and non-existence; he knows the scriptures, is the sixteen priests, the sacrifice, the ancestors, Vishnu, the Ashvins, and the fortress-destroyer (Indra).
The text describes a philosophical discourse on cosmic cycles and spiritual evolution.

supernatural_elements: Cosmic cycles of creation and destruction

extraction_text: The narrator explains that beings undergo cycles of creation and destruction lasting billions of years, measured metaphorically by the time to empty vast lakes drop by drop.
The narrator describes six colors (gunas/qualities) of life: black, brown, blue, red, yellow, and white, representing spiritual states.
Beings progress through these colors over countless rebirths, with black leading to hell and white representing the supreme, liberated state.

relationships: Divine beings determine destinations based on colors

extraction_text: The narrator details the transitions between colors: from black to brown after 100,000 years, from blue to red through wisdom and effort, and ultimately to white through pure actions.
The text mentions beings ascending to heaven, falling back to earth, and potentially regressing to lower states due to time's constraints.

relationships: Movement between heavenly, earthly, and hell realms

extraction_text: The ultimate white state is described as supreme, beyond the three gunas, achieved through 700 pure actions and passage through eight revered worlds.
Narada (referred to as '永童' in the text) explains the cycle of rebirth, ascension through higher worlds, and ultimate liberation to Vritra (弗栗多).
Vritra, upon hearing Narada's teaching, accepts its truth, becomes purified, and abandons his life to attain the supreme state.

attributes.action: Acceptance of teaching, Self-constraint, Attainment of liberation

extraction_text: Yudhishthira (坚战) identifies the deity described by Narada as Krishna (Janardana, 遮那陀那).
Bhishma (毗湿摩) explains that Krishna (Keshava, 盖沙婆) is an eighth part of the supreme deity Vishnu (毗湿奴), who creates and sustains the world.

supernatural_elements: Divine creation and sustenance of the world

extraction_text: Yudhishthira concludes that Vritra, having achieved a pure state and liberation, was joyful and free from rebirth, unlike those who fall into lower realms due to impure actions.

supernatural_elements: Contrast between liberation and rebirth in lower realms

extraction_text: Yudhishthira expresses confusion and asks Bhishma to explain how the righteous and devout Vritra was defeated by Indra.
In the past, Indra and the gods set out in their chariots and encountered Vritra standing before them like a mountain.

supernatural_elements: Vritra's immense size (500 yojanas tall, 300 yojanas wide)

extraction_text: Vritra's gigantic form terrified the gods and even Indra, causing his legs to stiffen with fear.
A great battle commenced between Indra and Vritra, terrifying the three worlds.

supernatural_elements: Use of divine weapons (swords, tridents, spears, bows, etc.)

extraction_text: Brahma, other gods, sages, Siddhas, Gandharvas, and Apsaras arrived in celestial chariots to witness the battle.
Vritra surrounded Indra in the sky and showered him with a rain of stones.
The gods countered by driving away Vritra's stone rain with a shower of arrows.
Vritra, possessing great illusory power, used his magic to confuse Indra in battle.
Afflicted by Vritra's assault, Indra became bewildered, but Sage Vasishtha chanted the Sama Veda to keep him conscious.
Sage Vasishtha encouraged Indra, reminding him of his strength and duty to destroy the enemies of the gods.
Vasistha helps Indra regain clarity and strength.

attributes.relationship: Sage aiding the king of gods

extraction_text: Indra uses wisdom and yogic power to overcome Vritra's illusions.
Brihaspati approaches Shiva to request Vritra's destruction for the world's benefit.
Shiva's power enters Vritra as 'heat' or 'fever' (tapas).
Vishnu enters Indra's vajra (thunderbolt).
Brihaspati, Vasistha, and other sages urge Indra to kill Vritra.
Shiva explains Vritra's power from Brahma's boon and advises Indra to use yogic power to kill him, noting his own power has already entered Vritra.

attributes.supernatural_element: Explanation of Vritra's boon and Shiva's prior action

extraction_text: Indra vows to kill Vritra with the vajra in Shiva's presence.
The 'heat' fully affects Vritra; gods and sages cheer; war drums sound; Asuras lose memory and wisdom.
Sages and gods praise and encourage Indra and Shiva as Indra stands ready for battle.

attributes.relationship: Divine and sage alliance against Asuras
